sections.b: The fourth and last use of the word in the Bible is 2 John 1:7: "many deceivers went out into the world, people who do not confess Jesus Christ as coming in the flesh. This one is the deceiver and the antichrist." As in 1 John, the antichrist here is not a single figure still to come but a description of teachers already at work, and the singular follows a plural: any such teacher, or all of them together, is "the antichrist" (Plummer). The test is a confession about Jesus, and the danger is that churches will give such teachers a welcome (2 John 1:10-11).

common: In John's letters "antichrist" names false teachers already present, not only one enemy at the end of history.

sections.h: 2 John: shutting the door on traveling deceivers
sections.b: 2 John gives a test and a rule. The test: whether a teacher confesses "Jesus Christ as coming in the flesh" (2 John 1:7) and "remains in the teaching of Christ" instead of "going ahead" beyond it (2 John 1:9). The rule: "do not take him into the house, and do not say 'Greetings!' to him" (2 John 1:10), since to welcome him is to share in his work. In a world of house churches and traveling teachers, the door of the house was where a false teacher could be stopped. The Didache gives a similar rule: a teacher who "turn and teach another doctrine to the destruction of this" is not to be heard (Didache 11.2).

common: Plummer read 2 John 10 as forbidding any act that would seem to approve a false teaching, not ordinary courtesy.
uncommon: Some early Christians read 2 John 10 as forbidding even conversation with heretics (Irenaeus' story of Polycarp and Marcion).

sections.h: 2 and 3 John: welcome and its limits
sections.b: The two short letters of the Elder are about whom to take in. 3 John praises Gaius for receiving traveling brothers, "strangers at that," and sending them on "in a way worthy of God" (3 John 1:5-8). 2 John forbids taking into the house a teacher who does not bring the teaching of Christ (2 John 1:10). Hospitality in these letters is not only kindness; it is support for a mission, and so it can be given to the truth or to its enemies.

2 John 1:10 tells the readers not to take a false teacher "into the house," with no "your" in the Greek. Many readers think of the house where the church met: to receive a traveling teacher there was to give him lodging, a hearing in the meeting and the church's approval. The letter is addressed to "the chosen lady and her children," which may itself picture a house church and its members.

2 John forbids taking into the house, or even greeting, a teacher who does not bring the teaching of Christ (2 John 1:10-11). Irenaeus quoted it; at the Council of Carthage in 256 Aurelius of Chullabi used it to argue that people who may not enter a house may not enter God's house without the church's baptism, while Stephen, bishop of Rome, ruled that people coming from a heresy were not to be baptized again (Cyprian, Letter 73). The Mennonite Dordrecht Confession (1632), which teaches shunning, does not use this letter: it bases shunning on 1 Corinthians 5 and 2 Thessalonians 3 and requires help for the shunned in need. Plummer read the rule as forbidding any act that would seem to approve the false teaching.

sections.h: 2 John: love that walks by the commands
sections.b: The Elder asks the chosen lady to keep the command "we have had from the beginning: that we love each other" (2 John 1:5), and defines love as obedience: "love means this: that we walk by his commands" (2 John 1:6). Love and truth are held together: he loves the readers "in truth" (2 John 1:1), and his love does not reach to welcoming those who deny the truth (2 John 1:10).

2 and 3 John open with "The Elder" and no name. Irenaeus quoted 2 John as the teaching of John, the Lord's disciple. Eusebius, building on Papias' mention of "the presbyter John," listed both letters as disputed, unsure "whether they belong to the evangelist or to another person of the same name," and Jerome reports that many in his day gave them to John the presbyter. Most scholars today think one man wrote both letters, from the same circle as 1 John and the Gospel.

Eusebius (about 325) wrote that 1 John was accepted without dispute, "but the other two are disputed." The Muratorian list counts two letters bearing John's name. Athanasius (367) and the councils of Hippo and Carthage list all three. The Syriac Peshitta left out 2 and 3 John (with 2 Peter, Jude and Revelation) until the Harklean version of 616. Lutheran usage still counts 2 and 3 John among the "antilegomena," the once-disputed books, while keeping them in the Bible.

2 John makes the confession that Jesus Christ comes "in the flesh" the test of a true teacher (2 John 1:7). 1 John 4:2 says he "has come"; 2 John uses a present, "coming," read as timeless, as pointing to his return, or as the same confession. Irenaeus describes Cerinthus, who divided the man Jesus from a heavenly "Christ" who left him before he suffered (Against Heresies 1.26.1): the kind of teaching the letter rejects.

2 John repeats 1 John's teaching in a few lines: the old command to love each other (2 John 1:5; 1 John 2:7-8), deceivers who have gone out into the world (2 John 1:7; 1 John 4:1), the confession of Jesus Christ in the flesh (2 John 1:7; 1 John 4:2-3), "This one is... the antichrist" (2 John 1:7; 1 John 2:22), having "both the Father and the Son" (2 John 1:9; 1 John 2:23), and joy filled up (2 John 1:12; 1 John 1:4). Where 1 John explains, 2 John applies: do not receive those who deny it.
